==Problem==

Right triangles <imath>T_1</imath> and <imath>T_2</imath>, have areas of 1 and 2, respectively. A side of <imath>T_1</imath> is congruent to a side of <imath>T_2</imath>, and a different side of <imath>T_1</imath> is congruent to a different side of <imath>T_2</imath>. What is the square of the product of the lengths of the other (third) sides of <imath>T_1</imath> and <imath>T_2</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }\frac{28}{3}\qquad\textbf{(B) }10\qquad\textbf{(C) }\frac{32}{3}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\frac{34}{3}\qquad\textbf{(E) }12</imath>

==Solution 1==

First of all, let the two sides which are congruent be <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath>, where <imath>y > x</imath>. The only way that the conditions of the problem can be satisfied is if <imath>x</imath> is the shorter leg of <imath>T_{2}</imath> and the longer leg of <imath>T_{1}</imath>, and <imath>y</imath> is the longer leg of <imath>T_{2}</imath> and the hypotenuse of <imath>T_{1}</imath>.

Notice that this means the value we are looking for is the square of <imath>\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \cdot \sqrt{y^{2}-x^{2}} = \sqrt{y^{4}-x^{4}}</imath>, which is just <imath>y^{4}-x^{4}</imath>.

The area conditions give us two equations: <imath>\frac{xy}{2} = 2</imath> and <imath>\frac{x\sqrt{y^{2}-x^{2}}}{2} = 1</imath>.

This means that <imath>y = \frac{4}{x}</imath> and that <imath>\frac{4}{x^{2}} = y^{2} - x^{2}</imath>.

Taking the second equation, we get <imath>x^{2}y^{2} - x^{4} = 4</imath>, so since <imath>xy = 4</imath>, <imath>x^{4} = 12</imath>.

Since <imath>y = \frac{4}{x}</imath>, we get <imath>y^{4} = \frac{256}{12} = \frac{64}{3}</imath>.

The value we are looking for is just <imath>y^{4}-x^{4} = \frac{64-36}{3} = \frac{28}{3}</imath> so the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }\frac{28}{3}}</imath>.

==Solution 2==
Like in Solution 1, we have <imath>\frac{xy}{2} = 2</imath> and <imath>\frac{x\sqrt{y^{2}-x^{2}}}{2} = 1</imath>.

Squaring both equations yields <imath>x^2y^2=16</imath> and <imath>x^2(y^2-x^2)=4</imath>.

Let <imath>a = x^2</imath> and <imath>b = y^2</imath>. Then <imath>b = \frac{16}{a}</imath>, and <imath>a\left(\frac{16}{a}-a\right)=4 \implies 16 - a^2 = 4 \implies a = 2\sqrt3</imath>, so <imath>b = \frac{16}{2\sqrt3} = \frac{8\sqrt3}{3}</imath>.

We are looking for the value of <imath>y^4 - x^4 = b^2 - a^2</imath>, so the answer is <imath>\frac{64}{3} - 12 = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }\frac{28}{3}}</imath>.

==Solution 3==

Firstly, let the right triangles be <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> and <imath>\triangle EDF</imath>, with <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> being the smaller triangle. As in Solution 1, let <imath>\overline{AB} = \overline{EF} = x</imath> and <imath>\overline{BC} = \overline{DF} = y</imath>. Additionally, let <imath>\overline{AC} = z</imath> and <imath>\overline{DE} = w</imath>.

We are given that <imath>[ABC] = 1</imath> and <imath>[EDF] = 2</imath>, so using <imath>\text{area} = \frac{bh}{2}</imath>, we have <imath>\frac{xy}{2} = 1</imath> and <imath>\frac{xw}{2} = 2</imath>. Dividing the two equations, we get <imath>\frac{xy}{xw}</imath> = <imath>\frac{y}{w} = 2</imath>, so <imath>y = 2w</imath>.

Thus <imath>\triangle EDF</imath> is a <imath>30^{\circ}-60^{\circ}-90^{\circ}</imath> right triangle, meaning that <imath>x = w\sqrt{3}</imath>. Now by the Pythagorean Theorem in <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>, <imath>\left(w\sqrt{3}\right)^2 + \left(2w\right)^2 = z^2 \Rightarrow 3w^2 + 4w^2 = z^2 \Rightarrow 7w^2 = z^2 \Rightarrow w\sqrt{7} = z</imath>.

The problem requires the square of the product of the third side lengths of each triangle, which is <imath>(wz)^2</imath>. By substitution, we see that <imath>wz</imath> = <imath>\left(w\right)\left(w\sqrt{7}\right) = w^2\sqrt{7}</imath>. We also know <imath>\frac{xw}{2} = 1 \Rightarrow\frac{(w)\left(w\sqrt{3}\right)}{2} =1 \Rightarrow (w)\left(w\sqrt{3}\right) = 2 \Rightarrow w^2\sqrt{3} = 2 \Rightarrow w^2 = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>. 

Since we want <imath>\left(w^2\sqrt{7}\right)^2</imath>, multiplying both sides by <imath>\sqrt{7}</imath> gets us <imath>w^2\sqrt{7} = \frac{2\sqrt{21}}{3}</imath>. Now squaring gives <imath>\left(\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{4*21}{9} = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }\frac{28}{3}}</imath>.

[Note: there is a mismatch of variables near the beginning that someone can fix: xw/2 is the area of the small triangle, which is actually the 30-60-90.]

==Solution 4 (brute force)==

This is a little more tedious than the other solutions, so it isn't preferable to be used in 
competition, but can be used if needed. We draw the two triangles, <imath>ABC</imath> and <imath>DEF</imath>, such that 
<imath>[ABC] = 1</imath> and <imath>[DEF] = 2</imath>. We denote the two sides <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath>. For <imath>DEF</imath>, <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are 
naturally the <imath>2</imath> shortest sides, both the legs. But for <imath>ABC</imath>, we would want <imath>x</imath> to be equal 
to one of its legs and <imath>y</imath> to be equal to the hypotenuse, to make the 2nd leg shorter (to make 
its area equal to <imath>1</imath>). 

So the 2nd leg's equation is <imath>\sqrt{x^2 - y^2}</imath> (using pythagorean theorem), and the 
hypotenuse of <imath>ABC</imath> is <imath>\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}</imath>. So we are trying to find 
<imath>\sqrt{x^2 - y^2} \cdot \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}</imath>. 

<cmath>\sqrt{x^2 - y^2} \cdot \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 - y^2)(x^2+y^2)} = \sqrt{x^4-y^4}</cmath>

Now, we know that <imath>[ABC]=1</imath>, so using <imath>\frac{b \cdot h}{2}=A</imath>, 
<imath>\frac{\sqrt{x^2 - y^2} \cdot y}{2}=1</imath>, and <imath>\sqrt{x^2 - y^2} \cdot y=2</imath>. 

We also know that <imath>[DEF]=2</imath>, so:
<cmath>\frac{xy}{2}=2 \implies xy=4 \implies x=\frac{4}{y}</cmath>

We substitute into our first equation, to get:
<cmath>\sqrt{\left(\frac{4}{y}\right)^2 - y^2} \cdot y=2</cmath>
<cmath>\implies \sqrt{\frac{16}{y^2} - y^2} \cdot y=2</cmath>
<cmath>\implies \sqrt{\frac{16-y^4}{y^2}} \cdot y=2</cmath>
<cmath>\implies \frac{\sqrt{16-y^4}}{y} \cdot y=2</cmath>
<cmath>\implies \sqrt{16-y^4}=2 \implies 16-y^4=4 \implies y^4=12 \implies y=12^{\frac{1}{4}}</cmath>

We plug this into <imath>xy=4</imath> to get <imath>x\left(12^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)=4</imath>, so <imath>x=\frac{4}{12^{\frac{1}{4}}}</imath>. 
We raise both sides to the 4th power, giving us:
<cmath>x^4=\frac{256}{12} \implies x^4=\frac{64}{3}</cmath>

Now we can put this into our <imath>\sqrt{x^4-y^4}</imath> equation, with <imath>y^4=12</imath> and <imath>x^4=\frac{64}{3}</imath>, to get:
<cmath>\sqrt{\frac{64}{3}-12} \implies \sqrt{\frac{64}{3}-\frac{36}{3}} \implies \sqrt{\frac{28}{3}}</cmath>

But remember that the problem is asking for the <imath>\textit{square}</imath> of the product of the 3rd side, 
so we square our product:
<cmath>\implies \left(\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}}\right)^2</cmath>

to finally get:
<cmath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) } \frac{28}{3}}</cmath>
